entries.bba6fc93091cf40a42b13c491b4275303e4f266c: <div sID="gen7135" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="2Kgs.4" sID="2Kgs.4"/> <div eID="gen7135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7136" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7137" type="x-p"/> Great service Elisha had done, in the foregoing chapter, for the three kings: to his prayers and prophecies they owed their lives and triumphs. One would have expected that the next chapter would tell us what honours and what dignities were conferred on Elisha for this, that he should immediately be preferred at court, and made prime-minister of state, that Jehoshaphat should take him home with him, and advance him in his kingdom. No, the wise man delivered the army, but no man remembered the wise man, <reference osisRef="Eccl.9.15">Eccl. ix. 15</reference>. Or, if he had preferment offered him, he declined it: he preferred the honour of doing good in the schools of the prophets before that of being great in the courts of princes. God magnified him, and that sufficed him—magnified him indeed, for we have him here employed in working no fewer than five miracles. I. He multiplied the poor widow's oil, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.1-2Kgs.4.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. He obtained for the good Shunammite the blessing of a son in her old age, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.8-2Kgs.4.17">ver. 8-17</reference>. III. He raised that child to life when it was dead, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.18-2Kgs.4.27">ver. 18-27</reference>. IV. He healed the deadly pottage, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.38-2Kgs.4.41">ver. 38-41</reference>. V. He fed 100 men with twenty small loaves, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.42-2Kgs.4.44">ver. 42-44</reference>.
entries.548081c9e14616298f3a0fa48709f04f7f374cbf: <div eID="gen7137" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7136" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Increase of the Widow's Oil. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 894.)</title> <div sID="gen7138" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets unto Elisha, saying, Thy servant my husband is dead; and thou knowest that thy servant did fear the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> : and the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen. <hi type="super">2</hi> And Elisha said unto her, What shall I do for thee? tell me, what hast thou in the house? And she said, Thine handmaid hath not any thing in the house, save a pot of oil. <hi type="super">3</hi> Then he said, Go, borrow thee vessels abroad of all thy neighbours, <hi type="italic">even</hi> empty vessels; borrow not a few. <hi type="super">4</hi> And when thou art come in, thou shalt shut the door upon thee and upon thy sons, and shalt pour out into all those vessels, and thou shalt set aside that which is full. <hi type="super">5</hi> So she went from him, and shut the door upon her and upon her sons, who brought <hi type="italic">the vessels</hi> to her; and she poured out. <hi type="super">6</hi> And it came to pass, when the vessels were full, that she said unto her son, Bring me yet a vessel. And he said unto her, <hi type="italic">There is</hi> not a vessel more. And the oil stayed. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then she came and told the man of God. And he said, Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest. <div eID="gen7138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7139" type="x-p"/> Elisha's miracles were for use, not for show; this recorded here was an act of real charity. Such also were the miracles of Christ, not only great wonders, but great favours to those for whom they were wrought. God magnifies his goodness with his power. <div eID="gen7139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7140" type="x-p"/> I. Elisha readily receives a poor widow's complaint. She was a prophet's widow; to whom therefore should she apply, but to him that was a father to the sons of the prophets, and concerned himself in the welfare of their families? It seems, the prophets had wives as well as the priests, though prophecy went not by entail, as the priesthood did. Marriage is honourable in all, and not inconsistent with the most sacred professions. Now, by the complaint of this poor woman (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.1">v. 1</reference>), we are given to understand, 1. That her husband, being <hi type="italic">one of the sons of the prophets,</hi> was well know to Elisha. Ministers of eminent gifts and stations should make themselves familiar with those that are every way their inferiors, and know their character and state. 2. That he had the reputation of a godly man. Elisha knew him to be one that feared the Lord, else he would have been unworthy of the honour and unfit for the work of a prophet. He was one that kept his integrity in a time of general apostasy, one of the 7000 that had not bowed the knee to Baal. 3. That he was dead, though a good man, a good minister. The prophets—do they live for ever? Those that were clothed with the Spirit of prophecy were not thereby armed against the stroke of death. 4. That he died poor, and in debt more than he was worth. He did not contract his debts by prodigality, and luxury, and riotous living, for he was one that feared the Lord, and therefore durst not allow himself in such courses: nay, religion obliges men not to live above what they have, nor to spend more than what God gives them, no, not in expenses otherwise lawful; for thereby, of necessity, they must disable themselves, at last, to give every one his own, and so prove guilty of a continued act of injustice all along. Yet it may be the lot of those that fear God to be in debt, and insolvent, through afflictive providences, losses by sea, or bad debts, or their own imprudence, for the <hi type="italic">children of light</hi> are not always <hi type="italic">wise for this world.</hi> Perhaps this prophet was impoverished by persecution: when Jezebel ruled, prophets had much ado to live, and especially if they had families. 5. That the creditors were very severe with her. Two sons she had to be the support of her widowed state, and their labour is reckoned <hi type="italic">assets</hi> in her hand; that must go therefore, and they must be bondmen for seven years (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.2">Exod. xxi. 2</reference>) to work out this debt. Those that leave their families under a load of debt disproportionable to their estates know not what trouble they entail. In this distress the poor widow goes to Elisha, in dependence upon the promise that the seed of the righteous shall not be forsaken. The generation of the upright may expect help from God's providence and countenance from his prophets. <div eID="gen7140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7141" type="x-p"/> II. He effectually relieves this poor widow's distress, and puts her in a way both to pay her debt and to maintain herself and her family. He did not say, <hi type="italic">Be warmed, be filled,</hi> but gave her real help. He did not give her some small matter for her present provision, but set her up in the world to sell oil, and put a stock into her hand to begin with. This was done by miracle, but it is an indication to us what is the best method of charity, and the greatest kindness one can do to poor people, which is, if possible, to help them into a way of improving what little they have by their own industry and ingenuity. <div eID="gen7141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7142" type="x-p"/> 1. He directed her what to do, considered her case: <hi type="italic">What shall I do for thee?</hi> The sons of the prophets were poor, and it would signify little to make a collection for her among them: but the God of the holy prophets is able to supply all her need; and, if she has a little committed to her management, her need must be supplied by his blessing and increasing that little. Elisha therefore enquired what she had to make money of, and found she had nothing to sell but one pot of oil, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.2">v. 2</reference>. If she had had any plate or furniture, he would have bidden her part with it, to enable her to be just to her creditors. We cannot reckon any thing really, nor comfortably, our own, but what is so when all our debts are paid. If she had not had this pot of oil, the divine power could have supplied her; but, having this, it will work upon this, and so teach us to make the best of what we have. The prophet, knowing her to have credit among her neighbours, bids her borrow of them <hi type="italic">empty vessels</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.3">v. 3</reference>), for, it seems, she had sold her own, towards the satisfying of her creditors. He directs her to shut the door upon herself and her sons, while she filled all those vessels out of that one. She must shut the door, to prevent interruptions from the creditors, and others while it was in the doing, that they might not seem proudly to boast of this miraculous supply, and that they might have opportunity for prayer and praise to God upon this extraordinary occasion. Observe, (1.) The oil was to be multiplied in the pouring, as the other widow's meal in the spending. The way to increase what we have is to use it; to him that so hath shall be given. It is not hoarding the talents, but trading with them, that doubles them. (2.) It must be poured out by herself, not by Elisha nor by any of the sons of the prophets, to intimate that it is in connexion with our own careful and diligent endeavours that we may expect the blessing of God to enrich us both for this world and the other. What we have will increase best in our own hand. <div eID="gen7142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7143" type="x-p"/> 2. She did it accordingly. She did not tell the prophet he designed to make a fool of her; but firmly believing the divine power and goodness, and in pure obedience to the prophet, she borrowed vessels large and many of her neighbours, and poured out her oil into them. One of her sons was employed to bring her empty vessels, and the other carefully to set aside those that were full, while they were all amazed to find their pot, like a fountain of living water, always flowing, and yet always full. They saw not the spring that supplied it, but believed it to be in him <hi type="italic">in whom all our springs are.</hi> Job's metaphor was now verified in the letter (<reference osisRef="Job.29.6">Job xxix. 6</reference>), <hi type="italic">The rock poured me out rivers of oil.</hi> Perhaps this was in the tribe of Asher, part of whose blessing it was that he should <hi type="italic">dip his foot in oil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.33.24">Deut. xxxiii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen7143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7144" type="x-p"/> 3. The oil continued flowing as long as she had any empty vessels to receive it; when every vessel was full the oil stayed (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.6">v. 6</reference>), for it was not fit that this precious liquor should run over, and be as water spilt on the ground, which cannot be gathered up again. Note, We are never straitened in God, in his power and bounty, and the riches of his grace; all our straitness is in ourselves. It is our faith that fails, not his promise. He gives above what we ask: were there more vessels, there is enough in God to fill them—enough for all, enough for each. Was not this pot of oil exhausted as long as there were any vessels to be filled from it? And shall we fear lest the golden oil which flows from the very root and fatness of the good olive should fail, as long as there are any lamps to be supplied from it? <reference osisRef="Zech.4.12">Zech. iv. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen7144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7145" type="x-p"/> 4. The prophet directed her what to do with the oil she had, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.7">v. 7</reference>. She must not keep it for her own use, to <hi type="italic">make her face to shine.</hi> Those whom Providence has made poor must be content with poor accommodations for themselves (this is <hi type="italic">knowing how to want</hi>), and must not think, when they get a little of that which is better than ordinary, to feed their own luxury: no, (1.) She must sell the oil to those that were rich, and could afford to bestow it on themselves. We may suppose, being produced by miracle, it was the best of its kind, like the wine (<reference osisRef="John.2.10">John ii. 10</reference>), so that she might have both a good price and a good market for it. Probably the merchants bought it to export, for oil was one of the commodities that Israel traded in, <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.17">Ezek. xxvii. 17</reference>. (2.) She must pay her debt with the money she received for her oil. Though her creditors were too rigorous with her, yet they must not therefore lose their debt. Her first care, now that she has wherewithal to do so, must be to discharge that, even before she makes any provision for her children. It is one of the fundamental laws of our religion that we render to all their due, pay every just debt, give every one his own, though we leave ever so little for ourselves; and this, not of constraint but willingly and without grudging; not only for wrath, to avoid being sued, but also for conscience' sake. Those that possess an honest mind cannot with pleasure eat their daily bread, unless it be their own bread. (3.) The rest must not be laid up, but she and her children must live upon it, not upon the oil, but upon the money received from it, with which they must put themselves into a capacity of getting an honest livelihood. No doubt she did as the man of God directed; and hence, [1.] Let those that are poor and in distress be encouraged to trust God for supply in the way of duty. <hi type="italic">Verily thou shalt be fed,</hi> though not feasted. It is true we cannot now expect miracles, yet we may expect mercies, if we wait on God and seek to him. Let widows particularly, and prophets' widows in a special manner, depend upon him to preserve them and their fatherless children alive, for to them he will be a husband, a father. [2.] Let those whom God has blessed with plenty use it for the glory of God and under the direction of his word: let them do justly with it, as this widow did, and serve God cheerfully in the use of it, and as Elisha, be ready to do good to those that need them, be eyes to the blind, and feet to the lame.
entries.ba2a07ba2f2c0252f134aeee1df19f5916d153f2: <div eID="gen7145" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Shunammite's Hospitality. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 893.)</title> <div sID="gen7146" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> And it fell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem, where <hi type="italic">was</hi> a great woman; and she constrained him to eat bread. And <hi type="italic">so</hi> it was, <hi type="italic">that</hi> as oft as he passed by, he turned in thither to eat bread. <hi type="super">9</hi> And she said unto her husband, Behold now, I perceive that this <hi type="italic">is</hi> a holy man of God, which passeth by us continually. <hi type="super">10</hi> Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall; and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick: and it shall be, when he cometh to us, that he shall turn in thither. <hi type="super">11</hi> And it fell on a day, that he came thither, and he turned into the chamber, and lay there. <hi type="super">12</hi> And he said to Gehazi his servant, Call this Shunammite. And when he had called her, she stood before him. <hi type="super">13</hi> And he said unto him, Say now unto her, Behold, thou hast been careful for us with all this care; what <hi type="italic">is</hi> to be done for thee? wouldest thou be spoken for to the king, or to the captain of the host? And she answered, I dwell among mine own people. <hi type="super">14</hi> And he said, What then <hi type="italic">is</hi> to be done for her? And Gehazi answered, Verily she hath no child, and her husband is old. <hi type="super">15</hi> And he said, Call her. And when he had called her, she stood in the door. <hi type="super">16</hi> And he said, About this season, according to the time of life, thou shalt embrace a son. And she said, Nay, my lord, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> man of God, do not lie unto thine handmaid. <hi type="super">17</hi> And the woman conceived, and bare a son at that season that Elisha had said unto her, according to the time of life. <div eID="gen7146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7147" type="x-p"/> The giving of a son to such as were old, and had been long childless, was an ancient instance of the divine power and favour, in the case of Abraham, and Isaac, and Manoah, and Elkanah; we find it here among the wonders wrought by Elisha. This was wrought in recompence for the kind entertainment which a good woman gave him, as the promise of a son was given to Abraham when he entertained angels. Observe here, <div eID="gen7147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7148" type="x-p"/> I. The kindness of the Shunammite woman to Elisha. Things are bad enough in Israel, yet not so bad but that God's prophet finds friends, wherever he goes. Shunem was a city in the tribe of Issachar, that lay in the road between Samaria and Carmel, a road that Elisha often travelled, as we find <reference osisRef="2Kgs.2.25">ch. ii. 25</reference>. <hi type="italic">There</hi> lived <hi type="italic">a great woman,</hi> who kept a good house, and was very hospitable, her husband having a good estate, and his heart safely trusting in her, and in her discreet management, <reference osisRef="Prov.31.11">Prov. xxxi. 11</reference>. So famous a man as Elisha could not pass and repass unobserved. Probably he had been accustomed to take some private obscure lodgings in the town; but this pious matron, having notice once of his being there, pressed him with great importunity, and, with much difficulty, constrained him to dine with her, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.8">v. 8</reference>. He was modest and loth to be troublesome, humble and affected not to associate with those of the first rank; so that it was not without some difficulty that he was first drawn into an acquaintance there; but afterwards, whenever he went that way in his circuit, he constantly called there. So well pleased was she with her guest, and so desirous of his company, that she would not only bid him welcome to her table, but provide a lodging-room for him in her house, that he might make the longer stay, not doubting but her house would be blessed for his sake, and all under her roof edified by his pious instructions and example—a good design, yet she would not do it without acquainting her husband, would neither lay out his money nor invite strangers to his house without his consent asked and obtained, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.9-2Kgs.4.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. She suggests to him, 1. That the stranger she would invite was a <hi type="italic">holy man of God,</hi> who therefore would do good to their family, and God would recompense the kindness done to him; perhaps she had heard how well paid the widow of Sarepta was for entertaining Elijah. 2. That the kindness she intended him would be no great charge to them; she would build him only a little chamber. Perhaps she had no spare room in the house, or none private and retired enough for him, who spent much of his time in contemplation, and cared not for being disturbed with the noise of the family. The furniture shall be very plain; no costly hangings, no stands, no couches, no looking-glasses, but a bed, and a table, a stool, and a candlestick, all that was needful for his convenience, not only for his repose, but for his study, his reading and writing. Elisha seemed highly pleased with these accommodations, for he turned in and lay there (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.11">v. 11</reference>), and, as it should seem, his man in the same chamber, for he was far from taking state. <div eID="gen7148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7149" type="x-p"/> II. Elisha's gratitude for this kindness. Being exceedingly pleased with the quietness of his apartment, and the friendliness of his entertainment, he began to consider with himself what recompence he should make her. Those that receive courtesies should study to return them; it ill becomes men of God to be ungrateful, or to sponge upon those that are generous. 1. He offered to use his interest for her in the king's court (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou hast been careful for us with all this care</hi> (thus did he magnify the kindness he received, as those that are humble are accustomed to do, though in the purse of one so rich, and in the breast of one so free, it was as nothing); now <hi type="italic">what shall be done for thee?</hi> As the liberal devise liberal things, so the grateful devise grateful things. "<hi type="italic">Wouldst thou be spoken for to the king, or the captain of the host,</hi> for an office for thy husband, civil or military? Hast thou any complaint to make, any petition to present, any suit at law depending, that needs the countenance of the high powers? Wherein can I serve thee?" It seems Elisha had got such an interest by his late services that, though he chose not to prefer himself by it, yet he was capable of preferring his friends. A good man can take as much pleasure in serving others as in raising himself. But she needs not any good offices of this kind to be done for her: <hi type="italic">I dwell</hi> (says she) <hi type="italic">among my own people,</hi> that is, "We are well off as we are, and do not aim at preferment." It is a happiness to <hi type="italic">dwell among our own people,</hi> that love and respect us, and to whom we are in a capacity of doing good; and a greater happiness to be content to do so, to be easy, and to know when we are well off. Why should those that live comfortably among their own people covet to live delicately in kings' palaces? It would be well with many if they did but know when they were well off. Some years after this we find this Shunammite had occasion to be spoken for to the king, though now she needed it not, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.3-2Kgs.8.4">ch. viii. 3, 4</reference>. Those that dwell among their own people must not think their mountain stands so strong as that it cannot be moved; they may be driven, as this good woman was, to sojourn among strangers. Our continuing city is above. 2. He did use his interest for her in the court of heaven, which was far better. Elisha consulted with his servant what kindness he should do for her, to such a freedom did this great prophet admit even his servant. Gehazi reminded him that she was childless, had a great estate, but no son to leave it to, and was past hopes of having any, her husband being old. If Elisha could obtain this favour from God for her, it would be the removal of that which at present was her only grievance. Those are the most welcome kindnesses which are most suited to our necessities. He sent for her immediately. She very humbly and respectfully <hi type="italic">stood in the door</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.15">v. 15</reference>), according to her accustomed modesty, and then he assured her that within a year she should bring forth a son, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.16">v. 16</reference>. She had received this prophet <hi type="italic">in the name of a prophet,</hi> and now she had not a courtier's reward, in being spoken for to the king, but a prophet's reward, a signal mercy given by prophets and in answer to prayer: the promise was a surprise to her, and she begged that she might not be flattered by it: "<hi type="italic">Nay, my lord, thou</hi> are <hi type="italic">a man of God,</hi> and therefore I hope speakest seriously, and doth not jest with me, nor lie unto thy handmaid." The event, within the time limited, confirmed the truth of the promise: <hi type="italic">She bore a son</hi> at the season that Elisha spoke of, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.17">v. 17</reference>. God built up her house, in reward to her kindness in building the prophet a chamber. We may well imagine what joy this brought to the family. <hi type="italic">Sing, O barren! thou that didst not bear.</hi>
entries.93caa0e0c026b2b99fd33823de1cdcf16ef5aeba: <div eID="gen7149" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Death of the Shunammite's Son; The Shunammite's Son Restored. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 887.)</title> <div sID="gen7150" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">18</hi> And when the child was grown, it fell on a day, that he went out to his father to the reapers. <hi type="super">19</hi> And he said unto his father, My head, my head. And he said to a lad, Carry him to his mother. <hi type="super">20</hi> And when he had taken him, and brought him to his mother, he sat on her knees till noon, and <hi type="italic">then</hi> died. <hi type="super">21</hi> And she went up, and laid him on the bed of the man of God, and shut <hi type="italic">the door</hi> upon him, and went out. <hi type="super">22</hi> And she called unto her husband, and said, Send me, I pray thee, one of the young men, and one of the asses, that I may run to the man of God, and come again. <hi type="super">23</hi> And he said, Wherefore wilt thou go to him to day? <hi type="italic">it is</hi> neither new moon, nor sabbath. And she said, <hi type="italic">It shall be</hi> well. <hi type="super">24</hi> Then she saddled an ass, and said to her servant, Drive, and go forward; slack not <hi type="italic">thy</hi> riding for me, except I bid thee. <hi type="super">25</hi> So she went and came unto the man of God to mount Carmel. And it came to pass, when the man of God saw her afar off, that he said to Gehazi his servant, Behold, <hi type="italic">yonder is</hi> that Shunammite: <hi type="super">26</hi> Run now, I pray thee, to meet her, and say unto her, <hi type="italic">Is it</hi> well with thee? <hi type="italic">is it</hi> well with thy husband? <hi type="italic">is it</hi> well with the child? And she answered, <hi type="italic">It is</hi> well. <hi type="super">27</hi> And when she came to the man of God to the hill, she caught him by the feet: but Gehazi came near to thrust her away. And the man of God said, Let her alone; for her soul <hi type="italic">is</hi> vexed within her: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath hid <hi type="italic">it</hi> from me, and hath not told me. <hi type="super">28</hi> Then she said, Did I desire a son of my lord? did I not say, Do not deceive me? <hi type="super">29</hi> Then he said to Gehazi, Gird up thy loins, and take my staff in thine hand, and go thy way: if thou meet any man, salute him not; and if any salute thee, answer him not again: and lay my staff upon the face of the child. <hi type="super">30</hi> And the mother of the child said, <hi type="italic">As</hi> the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> liveth, and <hi type="italic">as</hi> thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee. And he arose, and followed her. <hi type="super">31</hi> And Gehazi passed on before them, and laid the staff upon the face of the child; but <hi type="italic">there was</hi> neither voice, nor hearing. Wherefore he went again to meet him, and told him, saying, The child is not awaked. <hi type="super">32</hi> And when Elisha was come into the house, behold, the child was dead, <hi type="italic">and</hi> laid upon his bed. <hi type="super">33</hi> He went in therefore, and shut the door upon them twain, and prayed unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">34</hi> And he went up, and lay upon the child, and put his mouth upon his mouth, and his eyes upon his eyes, and his hands upon his hands: and he stretched himself upon the child; and the flesh of the child waxed warm. <hi type="super">35</hi> Then he returned, and walked in the house to and fro; and went up, and stretched himself upon him: and the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes. <hi type="super">36</hi> And he called Gehazi, and said, Call this Shunammite. So he called her. And when she was come in unto him, he said, Take up thy son. <hi type="super">37</hi> Then she went in, and fell at his feet, and bowed herself to the ground, and took up her son, and went out. <div eID="gen7150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7151" type="x-p"/> We may well suppose that, after the birth of this son, the prophet was doubly welcome to the good Shunammite. He had thought himself indebted to her, but henceforth, as long as she lives, she will think herself in his debt, and that she can never do too much for him. We may also suppose that the child was very dear to the prophet, as the son of his prayers, and very dear to the parents, as the son of their old age. But here is, <div eID="gen7151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7152" type="x-p"/> I. The sudden death of the child, though so much a darling. He was so far past the perils of infancy that he was able to go to the field to his father, who no doubt was pleased with his engaging talk, and his joy of his son was greater than the joy of his harvest; but either the cold or the heat of the open field overcame the child, who was bred tenderly, and he complained to his father that his head ached, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.19">v. 19</reference>. Whither should we go with our complaints, but to our heavenly Father? Thither the Spirit of adoption brings believers with all their grievances, all their desires, teaching them to cry, with groanings that cannot be uttered, "<hi type="italic">My head, my head;</hi> my heart, my heart." The father sent him to his mother's arms, his mother's lap, little suspecting any danger in his indisposition, but hoping he would drop asleep in his mother's bosom and awake well; but the sickness proved fatal; he slept the sleep of death (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.20">v. 20</reference>), was well in the morning and dead by noon: all the mother's care and tenderness could not keep him alive. A child of promise, a child of prayer, and given in love, yet taken away. Little children lie open to the arrests of sickness and death. But how admirably does the prudent pious mother guard her lips under this surprising affliction! Not one peevish murmuring word comes from her. She has a strong belief that the child will be raised to life again: like a genuine daughter of Abraham's faith, as well as loins, she accounts that God is able to raise him from the dead, for thence at first she <hi type="italic">received him in a figure,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.19">Heb. xi. 19</reference>. She had heard of the raising of the widow's son of Sarepta, and that the spirit of Elijah rested on Elisha; and such confidence had she of God's goodness that she was very ready to believe that he who so soon took away what he had given would restore what he had now taken away. By this faith <hi type="italic">women received their dead raised to life,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.11.35">Heb. xi. 35</reference>. In this faith she makes no preparation for the burial of her dead child, but for its resurrection; for she <hi type="italic">lays him on the prophet's bed</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.21">v. 21</reference>), expecting that he will stand her friend. <hi type="italic">O woman! great is thy faith.</hi> He that wrought it would not frustrate it. <div eID="gen7152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7153" type="x-p"/> II. The sorrowful mother's application to the prophet on this sad occasion; for it happened very opportunely that he was now at the college upon Mount Carmel, not far off. <div eID="gen7153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7154" type="x-p"/> 1. She begged leave of her husband to go to the prophet, yet not acquainting him with her errand, lest he should not have faith enough to let her go, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.22">v. 22</reference>. He objected, <hi type="italic">It is neither new moon nor sabbath</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.23">v. 23</reference>), which intimates that on those feasts of the Lord she used to go to the assembly in which he presided, with other good people, to hear the word, and to join with him in prayers and praises. She did not think it enough to have his help sometimes in her own family, but, though a great woman, attended on public worship, for which this was none of the times appointed; <hi type="italic">therefore,</hi> said the husband, "why wilt thou go to day? What is the matter?" "No harm," said she, "<hi type="italic">It shall be well,</hi> so you will say yourself hereafter." See how this husband and wife vied with each other in showing mutual regard; she was so dutiful to him that she would not go till she had acquainted him with her journey, and he so kind to her that he would not oppose it, though she did not think fit to acquaint him with her business. 2. She made all the haste she could to the prophet (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.24">v. 24</reference>), and he, seeing her at a distance, sent his servant to enquire whether any thing was amiss, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.25-2Kgs.4.26">v. 25, 26</reference>. The questions were particular: <hi type="italic">Is it well with thee? Is it well with thy husband? Is it well with the child?</hi> Note, It well becomes the men of God, with tenderness and concern, to enquire about the welfare of their friends and their families. The answer was general <hi type="italic">It is well.</hi> Gehazi was not the man that she came to complain to, and therefore she put him off with this; she said little, and little said is soon amended (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.1-Ps.39.2">Ps. xxxix. 1, 2</reference>), but what she did say was very patient: "It is well with me, with my husband, with the child"—all well, and yet the child dead in the house. Note, When God calls away our dearest relations by death it becomes us quietly to say, "It is well both with us and them;" it is well, for all is well that God does; all is well with those that are gone if they have gone to heaven, and all well with us that stay behind if by the affliction we are furthered in our way thither. 3. When she came to the prophet she humbly reasoned with him concerning her present affliction. She threw herself at his feet, as one troubled and in grief, which she never showed till she came to him who, she believed, could help her, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.27">v. 27</reference>. When her passion would do her service she knew how to discover it, as well as how to conceal it when it would do her disservice. Gehazi knew his master would not be pleased to see her lie at his feet, and therefore would have raised her up; but Elisha waited to hear from her, since he might not know immediately from God, what was the cause of her trouble. God discovered things to his prophets as he saw fit, not always as they desired; God did not show this to the prophet, because he might know it from the good woman herself. What she said was very pathetic. She appealed to the prophet, (1.) Concerning her indifference to this mercy which was now taken from her: "<hi type="italic">Did I desire a son of my lord?</hi> No, thou knowest I did not; it was thy own proposal, not mine; I did not fret for the want of a son, as Hannah, nor beg, as Rachel, <hi type="italic">Give me children or else I die.</hi>" Note, When any creature-comfort is taken from us, it is well if we can say, through grace, that we did not set our hearts inordinately upon it; for, if we did, we have reason to fear it was given in anger and taken away in wrath. (2.) Concerning her entire dependence upon the prophet's word: <hi type="italic">Did I not say, Do not deceive me?</hi> Yes, she did say so (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.16">v. 16</reference>), and this reflection upon it may be considered either, [1.] As quarrelling with the prophet for deceiving her. She was ready to think herself mocked with the mercy when it was so soon removed, and that it would have been better she had never had this child than to be deprived of him when she began to have comfort in him. Note, The loss of a mercy should not make us undervalue the gift of it. Or, [2.] As pleading with the prophet for the raising of the child to life again: "<hi type="italic">I said, Do not deceive me,</hi> and I know thou wilt not." Note, However the providence of God may disappoint us, we may be sure the promise of God never did, nor ever will, deceive us: hope in that will not make us ashamed. <div eID="gen7154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7155" type="x-p"/> III. The raising of the child to life again. We may suppose that the woman gave Elisha a more express account of the child's death, and he gave her a more express promise of his resurrection, than is here related, where we are briefly told, <div eID="gen7155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7156" type="x-p"/> 1. That Elisha sent Gehazi to go in all haste to the dead child, gave him his staff, and bade him lay that on the face of the child, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.29">v. 29</reference>. I know not what to make of this. Elisha knew that Elijah raised the dead child with a very close application, stretching himself upon the child, and praying again and again, and could he think to raise this child by so slight a ceremony as this, especially when nothing hindered him from coming himself? Shall such a power as this be delegated, and to no better man that Gehazi? Bishop Hall suggests that it was done out of human conceit, and not by divine instinct, and therefore it failed of the effect; God will not have such great favours made too cheap, nor shall they be too easily come by, lest they be undervalued. <div eID="gen7156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7157" type="x-p"/> 2. The woman resolved not to go back without the prophet himself (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.30">v. 30</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will not leave thee.</hi> She had no great expectation from the staff, she would have the hand, and she was in the right of it. Perhaps God intended hereby to teach us not to put that confidence in creatures, that are servants, which the power of the Creator, their Master and ours, will alone bear the weight of. Gehazi returns <hi type="italic">re infecta—without success,</hi> without the tidings of any sign of life in the child (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.31">v. 31</reference>): <hi type="italic">The child is not awaked,</hi> intimating, to the comfort of the mother, that its death was but a sleep, and that he expected that it would shortly be awaked. In the raising of dead souls to spiritual life ministers can do no more by their own power than Gehazi here could; they lay the word, like the prophet's staff, before their faces, but there is neither voice nor hearing, till Christ, by his Spirit, comes himself. The letter alone kills; it is the Spirit that gives life. It is not prophesying upon dry bones that will put life into them, breath must come from heaven and breathe upon those slain. <div eID="gen7157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7158" type="x-p"/> 3. The prophet, by earnest prayer, obtained from God the restoring of this dead child to life again. He found the child dead upon his own bed (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.32">v. 32</reference>), <hi type="italic">and shut the door upon them twain,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.33">v. 33</reference>. Even the dead child is spoken of as a person, one of the twain, for it was still in being and not lost. He shut out all company, that he might not seem to glory in the power God had given him, or to use it for ostentation and to be seen of men. Observe, <div eID="gen7158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7159" type="x-p"/> (1.) How closely the prophet applied himself to this great operation, perhaps being sensible that he had tempted God too much in thinking to effect it by the staff in Gehazi's hand, for which he thought himself rebuked by the disappointment. He now found it a harder task than he then thought, and therefore addressed himself to it with great solemnity. [1.] He <hi type="italic">prayed unto the Lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.33">v. 33</reference>), probably as Elijah had done, <hi type="italic">Let this child's soul come into him again.</hi> Christ raised the dead to life as one having authority—<hi type="italic">Damsel, arise—young man, I say unto thee, Arise—Lazarus, come forth</hi> (for he was powerful and faithful as a Son, the Lord of life), but Elijah and Elisha did it by petition, as servants. [2.] He <hi type="italic">lay upon the child</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.34">v. 34</reference>), as if he would communicate to him some of his vital heat or spirits. Thus he expressed the earnestness of his desire, and gave a sign of that divine power which he depended upon for the accomplishment of this great work. He first <hi type="italic">put his mouth to the child's mouth,</hi> as if, in God's name, he would breathe into him the breath of life; then <hi type="italic">his eyes to the child's eyes,</hi> to open them again to the light of life; then <hi type="italic">his hands to the child's hands,</hi> to put strength into them. He then <hi type="italic">returned, and walked in the house,</hi> as one full of care and concern, and wholly intent upon what he was about. Then he went up stairs again, and the second time, <hi type="italic">stretched himself upon the child,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.35">v. 35</reference>. Those that would be instrumental in conveying spiritual life to dead souls must thus affect themselves with their case, and accommodate themselves to it, and labour fervently in prayer for them. <div eID="gen7159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7160" type="x-p"/> (2.) How gradually the operation was performed. At the first application, <hi type="italic">the flesh of the child waxed warm</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.34">v. 34</reference>), which gave the prophet encouragement to continue instant in prayer. After a while, <hi type="italic">the child sneezed seven times,</hi> which was an indication, not only of life, but liveliness. Some have reported it as an ancient tradition that when God breathed into Adam the breath of life the first evidence of his being alive was sneezing, which gave rise to the usage of paying respect to those that sneeze. Some observe here that sneezing clears the head, and there lay the child's distemper. <div eID="gen7160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7161" type="x-p"/> (3.) How joyfully the child was restored alive to his mother (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.36-2Kgs.4.37">v. 36, 37</reference>), and all parties concerned <hi type="italic">were not a little comforted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.20.12">Acts xx. 12</reference>. See the power of God, who kills and makes alive again. See the power of prayer; as it has the key of the clouds, so it has the key of death. See the power of faith; that fixed law of nature (that death is a way whence there is no returning) shall rather be dispensed with than this believing Shunammite shall be disappointed.
entries.43b962550a5a1121d5985411224dcfb110e95e1b: <div eID="gen7161" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Miracle on the Poisoned Pottage; the Miracle on the Barley Loaves. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 887.)</title> <div sID="gen7162" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">38</hi> And Elisha came again to Gilgal: and <hi type="italic">there was</hi> a dearth in the land; and the sons of the prophets <hi type="italic">were</hi> sitting before him: and he said unto his servant, Set on the great pot, and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets. <hi type="super">39</hi> And one went out into the field to gather herbs, and found a wild vine, and gathered thereof wild gourds his lap full, and came and shred <hi type="italic">them</hi> into the pot of pottage: for they knew <hi type="italic">them</hi> not. <hi type="super">40</hi> So they poured out for the men to eat. And it came to pass, as they were eating of the pottage, that they cried out, and said, O <hi type="italic">thou</hi> man of God, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> death in the pot. And they could not eat <hi type="italic">thereof.</hi> <hi type="super">41</hi> But he said, Then bring meal. And he cast <hi type="italic">it</hi> into the pot; and he said, Pour out for the people, that they may eat. And there was no harm in the pot. <hi type="super">42</hi> And there came a man from Baal-shalisha, and brought the man of God bread of the firstfruits, twenty loaves of barley, and full ears of corn in the husk thereof. And he said, Give unto the people, that they may eat. <hi type="super">43</hi> And his servitor said, What, should I set this before an hundred men? He said again, Give the people, that they may eat: for thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , They shall eat, and shall leave <hi type="italic">thereof.</hi> <hi type="super">44</hi> So he set <hi type="italic">it</hi> before them, and they did eat, and left <hi type="italic">thereof,</hi> according to the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen7162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7163" type="x-p"/> We have here Elisha in his place, in his element, among the sons of the prophets, teaching them, and, as a father, providing for them; and happy it was for them that they had one over them who naturally cared for their state, under whom they were well fed and well taught. There was a dearth in the land, for the wickedness of those that dwelt therein, the same that we read of, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.1">ch. viii. 1</reference>. It continued seven years, just as long again as that in Elijah's time. A famine of bread there was, but not of hearing the word of God, for Elisha had the sons of the prophets sitting before him, to hear his wisdom, who were taught, that they might teach others. Two instances we have here of the care he took about their meat. Christ twice fed those to whom he preached. Elisha was in the more care about it now because of the dearth, that the sons of the prophets might not be ashamed in this evil time, but, even in <hi type="italic">the days of famine, might be satisfied,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.37.19">Ps. xxxvii. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen7163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7164" type="x-p"/> I. He made hurtful food to become safe and wholesome. 1. On the lecture-day, the sons of the prophets being all to attend, he ordered his servant to provide food for their bodies, while he was breaking to them the bread of life for their souls. Whether there was any flesh-meat for them does not appear; he orders only that pottage should be seethed for them of herbs, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.38">v. 38</reference>. The sons of the prophets should be examples of temperance and mortification, not desirous of dainties, but content with plain food. If they have neither savoury meats nor sweet meats, nay, if a mess of pottage be all the dinner, let them remember that this great prophet entertained himself and his guests no better. 2. One of the servitors, who was sent to gather herbs (which, it should seem, must serve instead of flesh for the pottage), by mistake brought in that which was noxious, or at least very nauseous, and shred it into the pottage: <hi type="italic">wild gourds</hi> they are called, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.39">v. 39</reference>. Some think it was <hi type="italic">coloquintida,</hi> a herb strongly cathartic, and, if not qualified, dangerous. The sons of the prophets, it seems, were better skilled in divinity than in natural philosophy, and read their Bibles more than their herbals. If any of the fruits of the earth be hurtful, we must look upon it as an effect of the curse (<hi type="italic">thorns and thistles shall it bring forth unto thee</hi>), for the original blessing made all good. 3. The guests complained to Elisha of the unwholesomeness of their food. Nature has given man the sense of tasting, not only that wholesome food may be pleasant, but that that which is unwholesome may be discovered before it comes to the stomach; the mouth tries meat by tasting it, <reference osisRef="Job.12.11">Job xii. 11</reference>. This pottage was soon found by the taste of it to be dangerous, so that they cried out, <hi type="italic">There is death in the pot,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.40">v. 40</reference>. The table often becomes a snare, and that which should be for our welfare proves a trap, which is a good reason why we should not feed ourselves without fear; when we are receiving the supports and comforts of life we must keep up an expectation of death and a fear of sin. 4. Elisha immediately cured the bad taste and prevented the bad consequences of this unwholesome pottage; as before he had healed the bitter waters with salt, so now the bitter broth with meal, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.41">v. 41</reference>. It is probable that there was meal in it before, but that was put in by a common hand, only to thicken the pottage; this was the same thing, but cast in by Elisha's hand, and with intent to heal the pottage, by which it appears that the change was not owing to the meal (that was the sign only, not the means), but to the divine power. Now all was well, not only no death, but no harm in the pot. We must acknowledge God's goodness in making our food wholesome and nourishing. <hi type="italic">I am the Lord that healeth thee.</hi> <div eID="gen7164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7165" type="x-p"/> II. He made a little food to go a great way. 1. Elisha had a present brought him of twenty barley-loaves and some ears of corn (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.42">v. 42</reference>), a present which, in those ages, would not be despicable at any time, but now in a special manner valuable, when there was a dearth in the land. It is said to be of <hi type="italic">the first-fruits,</hi> which was God's due out of their increase; and when the priests and Levites were all at Jerusalem, out of their reach, the religious people among them, with good reason, looked upon the prophets as God's receivers, and brought their first-fruits to them, which helped to maintain their schools. 2. Having freely received, he freely gave, ordering it all to be set before the sons of the prophets, reserving none for himself, none for the hereafter. "<hi type="italic">Let the morrow take thought for the things of itself,</hi> give it all to the people that they may eat." It well becomes the men of God to be generous and open-handed, and the fathers of the prophets to be liberal to the sons of the prophets. 3. Though the loaves were little, it is likely no more than what one man would ordinarily eat at a meal, yet with twenty of them he satisfied 100 men, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.43-2Kgs.4.44">v. 43, 44</reference>. His servant thought that to set so little meat before so many men was but to tantalize them, and shame his master for making so great an invitation to such short commons; but he in God's name, pronounced it a full meal for them, and so it proved; they did eat, and left thereof, not because their stomachs failed them, but because the bread increased in the eating. God has promised his church (<reference osisRef="Ps.132.15">Ps. cxxxii. 15</reference>) <hi type="italic">that he will abundantly bless her provision, and satisfy her poor with bread;</hi> for whom he feeds he fills, and what he blesses comes to much, as what he blows upon comes to little, <reference osisRef="Hag.1.9">Hag. i. 9</reference>. Christ's feeding his hearers was a miracle far beyond this; but both teach us that those who wait upon God in the way of duty may hope to be both protected and supplied by a particular care of divine Providence.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.4"/> <div eID="gen7165" type="x-p"/>

entries.1e0d015d4c6fb827fe3d40700e00b340351c3017: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3368"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen4733" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.1-2Kgs.4.7">2Ki 4:1-7</reference>. Elisha Augments the Widow's Oil.<div eID="gen4733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3368"/><hi type="bold">1. there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets--</hi>They were allowed to marry as well as the priests and Levites. Her husband, not enjoying the lucrative profits of business, had nothing but a professional income, which, in that irreligious age, would be precarious and very scanty, so that he was not in a condition to provide for his family.<div eID="gen4734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4735" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bondmen--</hi>By the enactment of the law, a creditor was entitled to claim the person and children of the insolvent debtor, and compel them to serve him as bondmen till the year of jubilee should set them free. <div eID="gen4735" type="x-p"/>
entries.00ad15b7886082cba8fc87f1c5288b41359d3780: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3369"/><div sID="gen4736" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3369"/><hi type="bold">2-4. a pot--</hi>or cruet of oil. This comprising her whole stock of domestic utensils, he directs her to borrow empty vessels not a few; then, secluding herself with her children, [the widow] was to pour oil from her cruse into the borrowed vessels, and, selling the oil, discharge the debt, and then maintain herself and family with the remainder. <div eID="gen4736" type="x-p"/>
entries.711f6ba910ab08377102a21a6c87be61a05a9599: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3370"/><div sID="gen4737" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3370"/><hi type="bold">6. the oil stayed--</hi>that is, ceased to multiply; the benevolent object for which the miracle had been wrought having been accomplished.<div eID="gen4737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4738" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.8-2Kgs.4.17">2Ki 4:8-17</reference>. Promises a Son to the Shunammite. <div eID="gen4738" type="x-p"/>
entries.73e456ae70d717f1cadeda9d09651b413274614d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3371"/><div sID="gen4739" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3371"/><hi type="bold">8. Elisha passed to Shunem--</hi>now Sulam, in the plain of Esdraelon, at the southwestern base of Little Hermon. The prophet, in his journey, was often entertained here by one of its pious and opulent inhabitants. <div eID="gen4739" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b6724daea5171e39ddb43a206e23c2319e200d0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3372"/><div sID="gen4740" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3372"/><hi type="bold">10. Let us make a little chamber--</hi>not build, but prepare it. She meant a room in the oleah, the porch, or gateway (<reference osisRef="2Sam.18.33">2Sa 18:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.19">1Ki 17:19</reference>), attached to the front of the house, leading into the court and inner apartments. The front of the house, excepting the door, is a dead wall, and hence this room is called a chamber in the wall. It is usually appropriated to the use of strangers, or lodgers for a night, and, from its seclusion, convenient for study or retirement. <div eID="gen4740" type="x-p"/>
entries.10bac77d3d5e36edb340fe805df8eee6d7d51e70: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3373"/><div sID="gen4741" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3373"/><hi type="bold">13-16. what is to be done for thee?--</hi>Wishing to testify his gratitude for the hospitable attentions of this family, he announced to her the birth of a son "about this time next year." The interest and importance of such an intelligence can only be estimated by considering that Oriental women, and Jewish in particular, connect ideas of disgrace with barrenness, and cherish a more ardent desire for children than women in any other part of the world (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.10-Gen.18.15">Ge 18:10-15</reference>).<div eID="gen4741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4742" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.18-2Kgs.4.37">2Ki 4:18-37</reference>. Raises Her Dead Son. <div eID="gen4742" type="x-p"/>
entries.daf56be0cb5ef6499a0c93c65763e028bf6c1996: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3374"/><div sID="gen4743" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3374"/><hi type="bold">19. My head, my head!--</hi>The cries of the boy, the part affected, and the season of the year, make it probable that he had been overtaken by a stroke of the sun. Pain, stupor, and inflammatory fever are the symptoms of the disease, which is often fatal. <div eID="gen4743" type="x-p"/>
entries.94566db85037884740a6338b7ecbe2025cbbe1e8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3375"/><div sID="gen4744" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3375"/><hi type="bold">22. she called unto her husband--</hi>Her heroic concealment of the death from her husband is not the least interesting feature of the story. <div eID="gen4744" type="x-p"/>
entries.601c8c2de5fb1aade55839e2b43554ceb6aed1d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3376"/><div sID="gen4745" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3376"/><hi type="bold">24. Drive, and go forward--</hi>It is usual for women to ride on asses, accompanied by a servant, who walks behind and drives the beast with his stick, goading the animal at the speed required by his mistress. The Shunammite had to ride a journey of five or six hours to the top of Carmel. <div eID="gen4745" type="x-p"/>
entries.e884f26b6c3813195b24c90b8f60c85b6346e7c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3377"/><div sID="gen4746" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3377"/><hi type="bold">26-28. And she answered, It is well--</hi>Her answer was purposely brief and vague to Gehazi, for she reserved a full disclosure of her loss for the ear of the prophet himself. She had met Gehazi at the foot of the hill, and she stopped not in her ascent till she had disburdened her heavy-laden spirit at Elisha's feet. The violent paroxysm of grief into which she fell on approaching him, appeared to Gehazi an act of disrespect to his master; he was preparing to remove her when the prophet's observant eye perceived that she was overwhelmed with some unknown cause of distress. How great is a mother's love! how wondrous are the works of Providence! The Shunammite had not sought a son from the prophet--her child was, in every respect, the free gift of God. Was she then allowed to rejoice in the possession for a little, only to be pierced with sorrow by seeing the corpse of the cherished boy? Perish, doubt and unbelief! This event happened that "the works of God should be made manifest" in His prophet, "and for the glory of God." <div eID="gen4746" type="x-p"/>
entries.cc915f73c05e708aa098fcd09f8fc5a5a064878b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3378"/><div sID="gen4747" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3378"/><hi type="bold">29-31. take my staff ... and lay ... upon the face of the child--</hi>The staff was probably an official rod of a certain form and size. Necromancers used to send their staff with orders to the messengers to let it come in contact with nothing by the way that might dissipate or destroy the virtue imparted to it. Some have thought that Elisha himself entertained similar ideas, and was under an impression that the actual application of his staff would serve as well as the touch of his hand. But this is an imputation dishonorable to the character of the prophet. He wished to teach the Shunammite, who obviously placed too great dependence upon him, a memorable lesson to look to God. By sending his servant forward to lay his staff on the child, he raised [the Shunammite's] expectations, but, at the same time, taught her that his own help was unavailing--"there was neither voice, nor hearing." The command, to salute no man by the way, showed the urgency of the mission, not simply as requiring the avoidance of the tedious and unnecessary greetings so common in the East (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.1">Lu 10:1</reference>), but the exercise of faith and prayer. The act of Gehazi was allowed to fail, in order to free the Shunammite, and the people of Israel at large, of the superstitious notion of supposing a miraculous virtue resided in any person, or in any rod, and to prove that it was only through earnest prayer and faith in the power of God and for His glory that this and every miracle was to be performed. <div eID="gen4747" type="x-p"/>
entries.5ae4f9493c51623ea8cfc46fb740c4b1a7d4e11b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3379"/><div sID="gen4748" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3379"/><hi type="bold">34. lay upon the child, &c.--</hi>(see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.21">1Ki 17:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.20.10">Ac 20:10</reference>). Although this contact with a dead body would communicate ceremonial uncleanness, yet, in performing the great moral duties of piety and benevolence, positive laws were sometimes dispensed with, particularly by the prophets. <div eID="gen4748" type="x-p"/>
entries.6fe9c0b5e3feb47e90d82b0cea102d85722666c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3380"/><div sID="gen4749" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3380"/><hi type="bold">35. the child sneezed seven times, and the child opened his eyes--</hi>These were the first acts of restored respiration, and they are described as successive steps. Miracles were for the most part performed instantaneously; but sometimes, also, they were advanced progressively towards completion (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.44">1Ki 18:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.45">45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.8.24">Mr 8:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.8.25">25</reference>).<div eID="gen4749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4750" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.38-2Kgs.4.41">2Ki 4:38-41</reference>. Purifies Deadly Pottage. <div eID="gen4750" type="x-p"/>
entries.7983a0adc863058fabd7ee03efa62da07d31a5b5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3381"/><div sID="gen4751" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3381"/><hi type="bold">38. there was a dearth in the land--</hi>(see on <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.1">2Ki 8:1</reference>).<div eID="gen4751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4752" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the sons of the prophets were sitting before him--</hi>When receiving instruction, the scholars sat under their masters. This refers to their being domiciled under the same roof (compare <reference osisRef="2Kgs.6.1">2Ki 6:1</reference>).<div eID="gen4752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4753" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Set on the great pot--</hi>As it is most likely that the Jewish would resemble the Egyptian "great pot," it is seen by the monumental paintings to have been a large goblet, with two long legs, which stood over the fire on the floor. The seethed pottage consisted of meat cut into small pieces, mixed with rice or meal and vegetables. <div eID="gen4753" type="x-p"/>
entries.bbbd3d436ae845617b4e7d65c0a83b1a98a29a48: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3382"/><div sID="gen4754" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3382"/><hi type="bold">39. went out into the field to gather herbs--</hi>Wild herbs are very extensively used by the people in the East, even by those who possess their own vegetable gardens. The fields are daily searched for mallow, asparagus, and other wild plants.<div eID="gen4754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4755" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wild vine--</hi>literally, "the vine of the field," supposed to be the colocynth, a cucumber, which, in its leaves, tendrils, and fruit, bears a strong resemblance to the wild vine. The "gourds," or fruit, are of the color and size of an orange bitter to the taste, causing colic, and exciting the nerves, eaten freely they would occasion such a derangement of the stomach and bowels as to be followed by death. The meal which Elisha poured into the pot was a symbolic sign that the noxious quality of the herbs was removed.<div eID="gen4755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4756" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">lap full--</hi>The hyke, or large cloak, is thrown loosely over the left shoulder and fastened under the right arm, so as to form a lap or apron.<div eID="gen4756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4757" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.42-2Kgs.4.44">2Ki 4:42-44</reference>. Satisfies a Hundred Men with Twenty Loaves. <div eID="gen4757" type="x-p"/>
entries.628defa019db6c7168821a6b7b44dca6a3a8a911: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3383"/><div sID="gen4758" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3383"/><hi type="bold">43. They shall eat, and shall leave thereof--</hi>This was not a miracle of Elisha, but only a prediction of one by the word of the Lord. Thus it differed widely from those of Christ (<reference osisRef="Matt.15.37">Mt 15:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.8.8">Mr 8:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.17">Lu 9:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.12">Joh 6:12</reference>). <chapter eID="2Kgs.4"/>

entries.6ec1aa9030b034d3f5da1e1bb5eabd0d6a8d1b6c: <div eID="gen12478" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen12479" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12480" type="x-p"/> A widow of one of the prophets, oppressed by a merciless creditor, applies to Elisha, who multiplies her oil; by a part of which she pays her debt, abut subsists on the rest, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.1-2Kgs.4.7">2Kgs 4:1-7</reference>. His entertainment at the house of a respectable woman in Shunem, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.8-2Kgs.4.10">2Kgs 4:8-10</reference>. He foretells to his hostess the birth of a son, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.11-2Kgs.4.17">2Kgs 4:11-17</reference>. After some years the child dies, and the mother goes to Elisha at Carmel; he comes to Shunem, and raises the child to life, vv. 18-37. He comes to Gilgal, and prevents the sons of the prophets from being poisoned by wild gourds, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.38-2Kgs.4.41">2Kgs 4:38-41</reference>. He multiplies a scanty provision, so as to make it sufficient to feed one hundred men, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.4.42-2Kgs.4.44">2Kgs 4:42-44</reference>. <div eID="gen12480" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12479" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12481" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen12481" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12482" type="x-p"/> Now there cried a certain woman - This woman, according to the Chaldee, Jarchi, and the rabbins, was the wife of Obadiah. <div eID="gen12482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12483" type="x-p"/> Sons of the prophets - תלמידי נבייא talmidey nebiyaiya, "disciples of the prophets:" so the Targum here, and in all other places where the words occur, and properly too. <div eID="gen12483" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12484" type="x-p"/> The creditor is come - This, says Jarchi, was Jehoram son of Ahab, who lent money on usury to Obadiah, because he had in the days of Ahab fed the Lord's prophets. The Targum says he borrowed money to feed these prophets, because he would not support them out of the property of Ahab. <div eID="gen12484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12485" type="x-p"/> To take unto him my two sons to be bondmen - Children, according to the laws of the Hebrews, were considered the property of their parents, who had a right to dispose of them for the payment of their debts. And in cases of poverty, the law permitted them, expressly, to sell both themselves and their children; <reference osisRef="Exo.21.7">Exo 21:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Lev.25.39">Lev 25:39</reference>. It was by an extension of this law, and by virtue of another, which authorized them to sell the thief who could not make restitution, <reference osisRef="Exo.22.3">Exo 22:3</reference>, that creditors were permitted to take the children of their debtors in payment. Although the law has not determined any thing precisely on this point, we see by this passage, and by several others, that this custom was common among the Hebrews. Isaiah refers to it very evidently, where he says, Which of my creditors is it to whom I have sold you? Behold, for your iniquities have ye sold yourselves; <reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Isa 50:1</reference>. And our Lord alludes to it, <reference osisRef="Mat.18.25">Mat 18:25</reference>, where he mentions the case of an insolvent debtor, Forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded Him to be Sold, and his Wife and Children, and all that he had; which shows that the custom continued among the Jews to the very end of their republic. The Romans, Athenians, and Asiatics in general had the same authority over their children as the Hebrews had: they sold them in time of poverty; and their creditors seized them as they would a sheep or an ox, or any household goods. Romulus gave the Romans an absolute power over their children which extended through the whole course of their lives, let them be in whatever situation they might. They could cast them into prison, beat, employ them as slaves in agriculture, sell them for slaves, or even take away their lives! - Dionys. Halicarn. lib. ii., pp. 96, 97. <div eID="gen12485" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12486" type="x-p"/> Numa Pompilius first moderated this law, by enacting, that if a son married with the consent of his father, he should no longer have power to sell him for debt. <div eID="gen12486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12487" type="x-p"/> The emperors Diocletian and Maximilian forbade freemen to be sold on account of debt: <div eID="gen12487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12488" type="x-p"/> Ob aes alienum servire liberos creditoribus, jura non patiuntur. - Vid. Lib. ob. aes C. de obligat. <div eID="gen12488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12489" type="x-p"/> The ancient Athenians had the same right over their children as the Romans; but Solon reformed this barbarous custom. - Vid. Plutarch in Solone. <div eID="gen12489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12490" type="x-p"/> The people of Asia had the same custom, which Lucullus endeavored to check, by moderating the laws respecting usury. <div eID="gen12490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12491" type="x-p"/> The Georgians may alienate their children; and their creditors have a right to sell the wives and children of their debtors, and thus exact the uttermost farthing of their debt. - Tavernier, lib. iii., c. 9. And we have reason to believe that this custom long prevailed among the inhabitants of the British isles. See Calmet here. <div eID="gen12491" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12492" type="x-p"/> In short, it appears to have been the custom of all the inhabitants of the earth. We have some remains of it yet in this country, in the senseless and pernicious custom of throwing a man into prison for debt, though his own industry and labor be absolutely necessary to discharge it, and these cannot be exercised within the loathsome and contagious walls of a prison.
entries.2e11f2caecfb289224b4a772d96c484664dfac38: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen12492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12493" type="x-p"/> Save a pot of oil - Oil was used as aliment, for anointing the body after bathing, and to anoint the dead. Some think that this pot of oil was what this widow had kept for her burial: see <reference osisRef="Mat.26.12">Mat 26:12</reference>.
entries.7c01f450b1ac8f356dc8ef65159ed667647fa56f: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen12493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12494" type="x-p"/> And the oil stayed - While there was a vessel to fill, there was oil sufficient; and it only ceased to flow when there was no vessel to receive it. This is a good emblem of the grace of God. While there is an empty, longing heart, there is a continual overflowing fountain of salvation. If we find in any place or at any time that the oil ceases to flow, it is because there are no empty vessels there, no souls hungering and thirsting for righteousness. We find fault with the dispensations of God's mercy, and ask, Why were the former days better than these? Were we as much in earnest for our salvation as our forefathers were for theirs, we should have equal supplies, and as much reason to sing aloud of Divine mercy.
entries.31cd19cd7eedc7705e17ecd346fa01aed8b06615: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen12494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12495" type="x-p"/> Go, sell the oil, and pay thy debt - He does not inveigh against the cruelty of this creditor, because the law and custom of the country gave him the authority on which he acted; and rather than permit a poor honest widow to have her children sold, or that even a Philistine should suffer loss who had given credit to a genuine Israelite, he would work a miracle to pay a debt which, in the course of providence, it was out of her power to discharge.
entries.dd72bab9859899459dc516dc9d859385b7b91fb8: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen12495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12496" type="x-p"/> Elisha passed to Shunem - This city was in the tribe of Issachar, to the south of the brook Kishon, and at the foot of Mount Tabor. <div eID="gen12496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12497" type="x-p"/> Where was a great woman - In Pirkey Rab. Eliezer, this woman is said to have been the sister of Abishag, the Shunammite, well known in the history of David. <div eID="gen12497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12498" type="x-p"/> Instead of great woman, the Chaldee has, a woman fearing sin; the Arabic, a woman eminent for piety before God. This made her truly great.
entries.e34352e925f9caedcad2c6f5a7f207e203a2d9c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen12498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12499" type="x-p"/> This is a holy man of God - That is, a prophet, as the Chaldee interprets it. <div eID="gen12499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12500" type="x-p"/> Which passeth by us continually - It probably lay in his way to some school of the prophets that he usually attended.
entries.5d9fb5c03caa30ac9e07f562f8d1b1dc40888d62: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen12500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12501" type="x-p"/> Let us make a little chamber - See the note upon <reference osisRef="Jdg.3.20">Jdg 3:20</reference> (note). As the woman was convinced that Elisha was a prophet, she knew that he must have need of more privacy than the general state of her house could afford; and therefore she proposes what she knew would be a great acquisition to him, as he could live in this little chamber in as much privacy as if he were in his own house. The bed, the table, the stool, and the candlestick, were really every thing he could need, by way of accommodation, in such circumstances.
entries.c7890b86e03dead26cf903cd41e99dd03c64c554: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen12501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12502" type="x-p"/> Gehazi his servant - This is the first time we hear of this very indifferent character.
entries.fb8c5a4040d452ad58acea8525ddd9450125612b: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen12502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12503" type="x-p"/> Wouldest thou be spoken for to the king - Elisha must have had considerable influence with the king, from the part he took in the late war with the Moabites. Jehoram had reason to believe that the prophet, under God, was the sole cause of his success, and therefore he could have no doubt that the king would grant him any reasonable request. <div eID="gen12503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12504" type="x-p"/> Or to the captain of the host? - As if he had said, Wilt thou that I should procure thee and thy husband a place at court, or get any of thy friends a post in the army? <div eID="gen12504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12505" type="x-p"/> I dwell among mine own people - I am perfectly satisfied and contented with my lot in life; I live on the best terms with my neighbors, and am here encompassed with my kindred, and feel no disposition to change my connections or place of abode. <div eID="gen12505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12506" type="x-p"/> How few are there like this woman on the earth! Who would not wish to be recommended to the king's notice, or get a post for a relative in the army, etc.? Who would not like to change the country for the town, and the rough manners of the inhabitants of the villages for the polished conversation and amusements of the court? Who is so contented with what he has as not to desire more? Who trembles at the prospect of riches; or believes there are any snares in an elevated state, or in the company and conversation of the great and honorable? How few are there that will not sacrifice every thing - peace, domestic comfort, their friends, their conscience, and their God - for money, honors, grandeur, and parade?
entries.eb623008a52743c6a195796e55b43affc096973f: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen12506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12507" type="x-p"/> What then is to be done for her? - It seems that the woman retired as soon as she had delivered the answer mentioned in the preceding verse.
entries.cbbdf94b415d3bff2174efd5a7da5c839fd1f39b: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen12507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12508" type="x-p"/> Thou shalt embrace a son - This promise, and the circumstances of the parties, are not very dissimilar to that relative to the birth of Isaac, and those of Abraham and Sarah. <div eID="gen12508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12509" type="x-p"/> Do not lie - That is, Let thy words become true; or, as the rabbins understand it, Do not mock me by giving me a son that shall soon be removed by death; but let me have one that shall survive me.
entries.a5569aad35d147f34f01b3ba78ecf773b510932e: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen12509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12510" type="x-p"/> When the child was grown - We know not of what age he was, very likely four or six, if not more years; for he could go out to the reapers in the harvest field, converse, etc.
entries.51e06f31b5850a69e390a66aed6bc4b183725e90: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen12510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12511" type="x-p"/> My head, my head - Probably affected by the coup de soleil, or sun stroke, which might, in so young a subject, soon occasion death, especially in that hot country.
entries.e442c9b55f6e1b4880bbb6938987f889b6e87919: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen12511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12512" type="x-p"/> Laid him on the bed of the man of God - She had no doubt heard that Elijah had raised the widow's son of Zarephath to life; and she believed that he who had obtained this gift from God for her, could obtain his restoration to life.
entries.74d486df7627bdbb1ba207aaa17030bd458c8928: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen12512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12513" type="x-p"/> Wherefore wilt thou go - She was a very prudent woman; she would not harass the feelings of her husband by informing him of the death of his son till she had tried the power of the prophet. Though the religion of the true God was not the religion of the state, yet there were no doubt multitudes of the people who continued to worship the true God alone, and were in the habit of going, as is here intimated, on new moons and Sabbaths, to consult the prophet.
entries.ee82863a738e8caf6c9317a28996fc7607062325: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen12513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12514" type="x-p"/> Drive, and go forward - It is customary in the East for a servant to walk along side or drive the ass his master rides. Sometimes he walks behind, and goads on the beast; and when it is to turn, he directs its head with the long pole of the goad. It is probably to this custom that the wise man alludes when he says, "I have seen servants on horses, and princes walking as servants on the earth," on the ground.
