entries.0627a3cdc58269a42f353225d19fa82ab22e229f: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen12514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12515" type="x-p"/> It is well - How strong was her faith in God and submission to his authority! Though the heaviest family affliction that could befall her and her husband had now taken place; yet, believing that it was a dispensation of Providence which was in itself neither unwise nor unkind, she said, It is well with me, with my husband, and with my child. We may farther remark that, in her days, the doctrine of reprobate infants had not disgraced the pure religion of the God of endless compassion. She had no doubts concerning the welfare of her child, even with respect to another world; and who but a pagan or a stoic can entertain a contrary doctrine?
entries.b5e2dd6ebfd6a01754a426ebbb714578d73489fb: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen12515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12516" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath hid it from me, and hath not told me - In reference to this point he had not now the discernment of spirits. This, and the gift of prophecy, were influences which God gave and suspended as his infinite wisdom saw good.
entries.9afc772bb2891e62378c0dc3b336c8c7c4def4f4: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen12516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12517" type="x-p"/> Did I desire a son of my lord? - I expressed no such wish to thee; I was contented and happy; and when thou didst promise me a son, did I not say, Do not deceive me? Do not mock me with a child which shall grow up to be attractive and engaging, but of whom I shall soon be deprived by death.
entries.791819b2d52a733ba269949c0d3d7496de024c6d: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen12517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12518" type="x-p"/> Salute him not - Make all the haste thou possibly canst, and lay my staff on the face of the child; he probably thought that it might be a case of mere suspended animation or a swoon, and that laying the staff on the face of the child might act as a stimulus to excite the animal motions.
entries.368b74f2d691905207f210e18c779d659083d8dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen12518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12519" type="x-p"/> I will not leave thee - The prophet it seems had no design to accompany her; he intended to wait for Gehazi's return; but as the woman was well assured the child was dead, she was determined not to return till she brought the prophet with her.
entries.2117943433225c16f87de5553ce6dabc3a2bface: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen12519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12520" type="x-p"/> Behold, the child was dead - The prophet then saw that the body and spirit of the child were separated.
entries.55ba2f97c75379d3f2aaa957db0e02bcef6a2cd0: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen12520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12521" type="x-p"/> Prayed unto the Lord - He had no power of his own by which he could restore the child.
entries.333087898244f3010f696d0a3a23a360c9ba5876: <hi type="bold">Verse 34</hi> <div eID="gen12521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12522" type="x-p"/> Lay upon the child - Endeavored to convey a portion of his own natural warmth to the body of the child; and probably endeavored, by blowing into the child's mouth, to inflate the lungs, and restore respiration. He uses every natural means in his power to restore life, while praying to the Author of it to exert a miraculous influence. Natural means are in our power; those that are supernatural belong to God. We should always do our own work, and beg of God to do his.
entries.d468b41d6637aad3cb2c8d4418af7403f2f6d64d: <hi type="bold">Verse 35</hi> <div eID="gen12522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12523" type="x-p"/> The child sneezed seven times - That is, it sneezed abundantly. When the nervous influence began to act on the muscular system, before the circulation could be in every part restored, particular muscles, if not the whole body, would be thrown into strong contractions and shiverings, and sternutation or sneezing would be a natural consequence; particularly as obstructions must have taken place in the head and its vessels, because of the disorder of which the child died. Most people, as well as philosophers and physicians, have remarked how beneficial sneezings are to the removal of obstructions in the head. Sternutamenta, says Pliny, Hist. Nat., lib. xxviii., cap. 6, gravedinem capitis emendant; "Sneezing relieves disorders of the head."
entries.c7f62f98a8ee09fde47f70d2b3ca5eec40db41f5: <hi type="bold">Verse 37</hi> <div eID="gen12523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12524" type="x-p"/> She went in and fell at his feet - Few can enter into the feelings of this noble woman. What suspense must she have felt during the time that the prophet was employed in the slow process referred to above! for slow in its own nature it must have been, and exceedingly exhausting to the prophet himself.
entries.e884d16312d5dc4d5b06cb45de504b6ea7a2d81f: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen12524" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12525" type="x-p"/> Came again to Gilgal - He had been there before with his master, a short time prior to his translation. <div eID="gen12525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12526" type="x-p"/> Set on the great pot and seethe pottage for the sons of the prophets - It was in a time of dearth, and all might now stand in need of refreshment; and it appears that the prophet was led to put forth the power he had from God to make a plentiful provision for those who were present. The father of the celebrated Dr. Young, author of the Night Thoughts, preaching a charity sermon for the benefit of the sons of the clergy, took the above words for his text; nor could they be said to be inappropriate.
entries.c86a606241c2e5dd5a97a78c8a9e5b3f8f333273: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen12526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12527" type="x-p"/> Wild gourds - This is generally thought to be the coloquintida, the fruit of a plant of the same name, about the size of a large orange. It is brought hither from the Levant, and is often known by the name of the bitter apple; both the seeds and pulp are intensely bitter, and violently purgative. It ranks among vegetable poisons, as all intense bitters do; but, judiciously employed, it is of considerable use in medicine.
entries.a5ac7cabf599c0d354dca88c03665d3dd81a1797: <hi type="bold">Verse 40</hi> <div eID="gen12527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12528" type="x-p"/> There is death in the pot - As if they had said, "We have here a deadly mixture; if we eat of it, we shall all die."
entries.bb3c8048b2b8d3732af68af7c4f6bea51cc8423d: <hi type="bold">Verse 41</hi> <div eID="gen12528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12529" type="x-p"/> Bring meal - Though this might, in some measure, correct the strong acrid and purgative quality; yet it was only a miracle which could make a lapful of this fruit shred into pottage salutary.
entries.e298c1cd60d8fe0d53666dc2c54b5d0d963b1096: <hi type="bold">Verse 42</hi> <div eID="gen12529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12530" type="x-p"/> Bread of the first-fruits - This was an offering to the prophet, as the first-fruits themselves were an offering to God. <div eID="gen12530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12531" type="x-p"/> Corn in the husk - Probably parched corn or corn to be parched, a very frequent food in the East; full ears, before they are ripe, parched on the fire.
entries.495b6584620ad1156bfa39ac473ee6932c600a5a: <hi type="bold">Verse 43</hi> <div eID="gen12531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12532" type="x-p"/> Thus saith the Lord, They shall eat, and shall leave thereof - It was God, not the prophet, who fed one hundred men with these twenty loaves, etc. This is something like our Lord's feeding the multitude miraculously. Indeed, there are many things in this chapter similar to facts in our Lord's history: and this prophet might be more aptly considered a type of our Lord, than most of the other persons in the Scriptures who have been thus honored.  <chapter eID="2Kgs.4"/> <div eID="gen12532" type="x-p"/>

entries.ead518a7ed1e857a8016164287b331f10a5fa9a2: 2Ki 4:1-7 <div eID="gen5161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5162" type="x-p"/> The Widow’s Cruse of Oil. - A poor widow of the scholars of the prophets complained to Elisha of her distress, namely, that a creditor was about to take her two sons as servants (slaves). The Mosaic law gave a creditor the right to claim the person and children of a debtor who was unable to pay, and they were obliged to serve him as slaves till the year of jubilee, when they were once more set free (<reference osisRef="Lev.25.39-Lev.25.40">Lev 25:39-40</reference>). When the prophet learned, on inquiry that she had nothing in her house but a small flask of oil (אסוּך, from סוּך, means an anointing flask, a small vessel for the oil necessary for anointing the body), he told her to beg of all her neighbours empty vessels, not a few (אל־תּמעיטי, make not few, sc. to beg), and then to shut herself in with her sons, and to pour from her flask of oil into all these vessels till they were full, and then to sell this oil and pay her debt with the money, and use the rest for the maintenance of herself and her children. She was to close the house-door, that she might not be disturbed in her occupation by other people, and also generally to avoid all needless observation while the miracle was being performed. תּסּיאי המּלא, let that which is filled be put on one side, namely by the sons, who handed her the vessels, according to 2Ki 4:5 and 2Ki 4:6, so that she was able to pour without intermission. The form מיצקת is a participle <hi type="italic">Piel</hi>, and is quite appropriate as an emphatic form; the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> השּׁקת (<hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi>) is an unnecessary alteration, especially as the <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> of יצק is הצּיּק. השׁמן ויּעמד, then the oil stood, i.e., it ceased to flow. The <hi type="italic">asyndeton</hi> בניך ואתּ is very harsh, and the <hi type="italic">Vav copul</hi>. has probably dropped out. With the alteration proposed by L. de Dieu, viz., of ואתּ into ואת, “live with thy sons,” the verb תּחיי would necessarily stand first (Thenius).
entries.e74660c7419665545d977bb7eda35102c0ee33ff: 2Ki 4:8 <div eID="gen5162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5163" type="x-p"/> The Shunammite and her Son. - 2Ki 4:8. When Elisha was going one day (lit., <hi type="italic">the</hi> day, i.e., at that time, then) to <hi type="italic">Shunem</hi> (<hi type="italic">Solam</hi>, at the south-western foot of the Lesser Hermon; see at 1Ki 1:3), a wealthy woman (גּדולה as in <reference osisRef="1Sam.25.2">1Sa 25:2</reference>, etc.) constrained him to eat at her house; whereupon, as often as he passed by that place in his subsequent journeys from Carmel to Jezreel and back, he was accustomed to call upon her (סוּר as in <reference osisRef="Gen.19.2">Gen 19:2</reference>).
entries.ed8a3d03fa456e105ed0bdf4925e75a14728e25e: 2Ki 4:9-10 <div eID="gen5163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5164" type="x-p"/> The woman then asked her husband to build a small upper chamber for this holy man of God, and to furnish it with the necessary articles of furniture (viz., bed, table, seat, and lamp), that he might always turn in at their house. עליּת־קיר is either a walled upper chamber, i.e., one built with brick and not with wooden walls (Cler., Then.), or an upper chamber built upon the wall of the house (Ges.).
entries.28fcadf8e31a3e51c96f9f6c389afca560c080da: 2Ki 4:11-13 <div eID="gen5164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5165" type="x-p"/> After some time, when Elisha had spent the night in the chamber provided for him, he wanted to make some acknowledgment to his hostess for the love which she had shown him, and told his servant Gehazi to call her, and say to her: “Thou hast taken all this care for us, what shall I do to thee? Hast thou (anything) to say to the king or the chief captain?” i.e., hast thou any wish that I could convey to them, and intercede for thee? There is something striking here in the fact that Elisha did not address the woman himself, as she was standing before him, but told her servant to announce to her his willingness to make some return for what she had done. This was, probably, simply from a regard to the great awe which she had of the “holy man of God” (2Ki 4:9), and to inspire her with courage to give expression to the wishes of her heart.<note placement="foot">The conjecture that Elisha would not speak to her directly for the sake of maintaining his dignity, or that the historian looked upon such conversation with women as unbecoming in a teacher of the law (Thenius), is already proved to be untenable by 2Ki 4:15, 2Ki 4:16, where Elisha does speak to her directly.</note> <div eID="gen5165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5166" type="x-p"/> She answered: “I dwell among my people,” i.e., not, I merely belong to the people (Thenius), but, I live quietly and peaceably among my countrymen, so that I have no need for any intercession with the king and great men of the kingdom. Ἀπραγμοσύνῃ χαίρω καὶ εἰρηνικῶς διάγω καὶ πρός τινα ἀμφισβήτησιν ούκ ἀνέχομαι (Theodoret).
entries.b7e7b02b641444b1f441dc67f3d484a17878dbd6: 2Ki 4:14-16 <div eID="gen5166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5167" type="x-p"/> When Elisha conversed with Gehazi still further on the matter, the latter said: “But she has no son, and her husband is old.” Elisha then had her called again, and told her when she had entered the door: “At this time a year hence (חיּה כּעת, lit., at the time when it revives again; see at <reference osisRef="Gen.18.10">Gen 18:10</reference>) thou wilt embrace a son.” The same favour was to be granted to the Shunammite as that which Sarah had received in her old age, that she might learn that the God of Abraham still ruled in and for Israel. She replied: “No, my lord, thou man of God,” אל־תּכזּב, I do not excite in thy servant any deceptive hopes.
entries.1ba9e3c6f83fc465fec945c644bde57f0278e6b2: 2Ki 4:17 <div eID="gen5167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5168" type="x-p"/> But however incredible this promise might appear to her, as it had formerly done to Sarah (<reference osisRef="Gen.18.12-Gen.18.13">Gen 18:12-13</reference>), it was fulfilled at the appointed time (cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.21.2">Gen 21:2</reference>).
entries.32dbc532dcd7f22d508866a5662cfadedcc25acf: 2Ki 4:18-20 <div eID="gen5168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5169" type="x-p"/> But even the faith of the pious woman was soon to be put to the test, and to be confirmed by a still more glorious revelation of the omnipotence of the Lord, who works through the medium of His prophets. When the child presented to her by God had grown up into a lad, he complained one day to the reapers of the field of a violent headache, saying to his father, “My head, my head!” He was then taken home to his mother, and died at noon upon her knees, no doubt from inflammation of the brain produced by a sunstroke.
entries.7cfdc937ecd65331a2a6564edf93b2c95aa1a9ec: 2Ki 4:21-23 <div eID="gen5169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5170" type="x-p"/> The mother took the dead child at once up to the chamber built for Elisha, laid it upon the bed of the man of God, and shut the door behind her; she then asked her husband, without telling him of the death of the boy, to send a young man with a she-ass, that she might ride as quickly as possible to the man of God; and when her husband asked her, “Wherefore wilt thou go to him to-day, since it is neither new moon nor Sabbath?”<note placement="foot">From these words, Theod., Kimchi, C. a Lap., Vatabl., and others have drawn the correct conclusion, that the pious in Israel were accustomed to meet together at the prophets’ houses for worship and edification, on those days which were appointed in the law (<reference osisRef="Lev.23.3">Lev 23:3</reference>; Num 28:11.) for the worship of God; and from this Hertz and <hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi> have still further inferred, that in the kingdom of the ten tribes not only were the Sabbath and new moons kept, as is evident from <reference osisRef="Amos.8.5">Amo 8:5</reference> also, but the prophets supplied the pious in that kingdom with a substitute for the missing Levitical priesthood.</note> she replied, <hi type="italic">shalom</hi>; i.e., either “it is all well,” or “never mind.” For this word, which is used in reply to a question after one’s health (see 2Ki 4:26), is apparently also used, as Clericus has correctly observed, when the object is to avoid giving a definite answer to any one, and yet at the same time to satisfy him.
entries.f4965b9ff8d0ee0aa4cceb3909752d5bc6b592b4: 2Ki 4:24-25 <div eID="gen5170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5171" type="x-p"/> She then rode without stopping, upon the animal driven by the young man, to Elisha at mount Carmel. לרכּב אל־תּעצר־לי, literally, do not hinder me from riding.
entries.b85a60575311df1aa08fcce06c377c522b8a192a: 2Ki 4:28 <div eID="gen5172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5173" type="x-p"/> The pious woman then uttered this complaint to the prophet: “Did I ask a son of the Lord? Did I not say, Do not deceive me?” What had happened to her she did not say, - a fact which may easily be explained on psychological grounds from her deep sorrow, - but Elisha could not fail to discover it from what she said.
entries.fa45be7de92a100c555c7b88034fddaf07d026cf: 2Ki 4:29 <div eID="gen5173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5174" type="x-p"/> He therefore directed his servant Gehazi: “Gird thy loins and take thy staff in thy hand and go: if thou meet any one, thou wilt not salute him; and if any one salute thee, thou wilt not answer him; and lay my staff upon the face of the boy.” The object of this command neither to salute nor to return salutations by the way, was not merely to ensure the greatest haste (Thenius and many others), inasmuch as the people of the East lose a great deal of time in prolonged salutations (Niebuhr, <hi type="italic">Beschr. v. Arab</hi>. p. 48),<note placement="foot">Or, as C. a Lap. supposes: “that Gehazi might avoid all distraction of either eyes or ears, and prepare himself entirely by prayers for the accomplishment of so great a miracle.” Theodoret explains it in a similar manner: “He knew that he was vainglorious and fond of praise, and that he would be sure to tell the reason of his journey to those who should meet him by the way. And vainglory is a hindrance to thaumaturgy.”</note> but the prophet wished thereby to preclude at the very outset the possibility of attributing the failure of Gehazi’s attempt to awaken the child to any external or accidental circumstance of this kind. For since it is inconceivable that the prophet should have adopted a wrong method, that is to say, should have sent Gehazi with the hope that he would restore the dead boy to life, his only intention in sending the servant must have been to give to the Shunammite and her family, and possibly also to Gehazi himself, a practical proof that the power to work miracles was not connected in any magical way with his person or his staff, but that miracles as works of divine omnipotence could only be wrought through faith and prayer; not indeed with the secondary intention of showing that he alone could work miracles, and so of increasing his own importance (Köster), but to purify the faith of the godly from erroneous ideas, and elevate them from superstitious reliance upon his own human person to true reliance upon the Lord God.
entries.3c40ed29831dbce484d7adfd789bd265928721a1: 2Ki 4:30 <div eID="gen5174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5175" type="x-p"/> The mother of the boy does not appear, indeed, to have anticipated any result from the measures adopted by Elisha; for she swears most solemnly that she will not leave him. But the question arises, whether this urging of the prophet to come himself and help arose from doubt as to the result of Gehazi’s mission, or whether it was not rather an involuntary utterance of her excessive grief, and of the warmest wish of her maternal heart to see her beloved child recalled to life. We may probably infer the latter from the fulfilment of her request by Elisha.
entries.4ac6dd386c6338e98f7faf0a7f6d7f296ca7e021: 2Ki 4:31 <div eID="gen5175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5176" type="x-p"/> Gehazi did as he was commanded, but the dead child did not come to life again; the prophet’s staff worked no miracle. “There was no sound and no attention,” i.e., the dead one gave no sign of life. This is the meaning of קשׁב ואין קול אין both here and 1Ki 18:29, where it is used of dead idols. The attempt of Gehazi to awaken the child was unsuccessful, not <hi type="italic">propter fidem ipsi a muliere non adhibitam</hi> (Seb. Schm.), nor because of the vainglory of Gehazi himself, but simply to promote in the godly of Israel true faith in the Lord.
entries.773087c1d00f8afb69afd629f44cbba50e5ae7bb: 2Ki 4:32-35 <div eID="gen5176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5177" type="x-p"/> Elisha then entered the house, where the boy was lying dead upon his bed, and shut the door behind them both (i.e., himself and the dead child), and prayed to the Lord. He then lay down upon the boy, so that his mouth, his eyes, and his hands lay upon the mouth, eyes, and hands of the child, bowing down over him (גּהר; see at 1Ki 18:42); and the flesh (the body) of the child became warm. He then turned round, i.e., turned away from the boy, went once up and down in the room, and bowed himself over him again; whereupon the boy sneezed seven times, and then opened his eyes. This raising of the dead boy to life does indeed resemble the raising of the dead by Elijah (1Ki 17:20.); but it differs so obviously in the manner in which it was effected, that we may see at once from this that Elisha did not possess the double measure of the spirit of Elijah. It is true that Elijah stretched himself three times upon the dead child, but at his prayer the dead returned immediately to life, whereas in the case of Elisha the restoration to life was a gradual thing.<note placement="foot">The raising of the dead by Elijah and Elisha, especially by the latter, has been explained by many persons as being merely a revivification by magnetic manipulations or by the force of animal magnetism (even Passavant and Ennemoser adopt this view). But no dead person was ever raised to life by animal magnetism; and the assumption that the two boys were only apparently dead is at variance with the distinct words of the text, in addition to which, both Elisha and Elijah accomplished the miracle through their prayer, as is stated as clearly as possible both here (2Ki 4:33) and also at 1Ki 17:21-22.</note> <div eID="gen5177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5178" type="x-p"/> And they both differ essentially from the raising of the dead by Christ, who recalled the dead to life by one word of His omnipotence (<reference osisRef="Mark.5.39-Mark.5.42">Mar 5:39-42</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.7.13-Luke.7.15">Luk 7:13-15</reference>; Joh 11:43-44), a sign that He was the only-begotten Son of God, to whom the Father gave to have life in Himself, even as the Father has life in Himself (Joh 5:25.), in whose name the Apostle Peter also was able through prayer to recall the dead Tabitha to life, whereas Elisha and Elijah had only to prophesy by word and deed of the future revelation of the glory of God.
entries.867bc0b60f03942553cdc2f382924df75544616d: 2Ki 4:36-37 <div eID="gen5178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5179" type="x-p"/> After the restoration of the boy to life, Elisha had his mother called and gave her back her son, for which she fell at his feet with thanksgiving.
entries.2e7443f41f95c1634a62550e17184fd07d6fcfb2: 2Ki 4:38 <div eID="gen5179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5180" type="x-p"/> Elisha Makes Uneatable Food Wholesome. - 2Ki 4:38. When Elisha had returned to Gilgal, the seat of a school of the prophets (see at 2Ki 2:1), i.e., had come thither once more on his yearly circuit, during the famine which prevailed in the land (see at 2Ki 8:1), and the prophets’ scholars sat before him (the teacher and master), he directed his servant (i.e., probably not Gehazi, but the pupil who waited upon him) to put the large pot to the fire and boil a dish for the pupils of the prophets. שׁפט answers to the German <hi type="italic">beisetzen</hi>, which is used for placing a vessel <hi type="italic">upon</hi> the fire (cf. <reference osisRef="Ezek.24.3">Eze 24:3</reference>).
entries.d050469700e5e7ae4f570b267054cdff0ea034d0: 2Ki 4:39 <div eID="gen5180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5181" type="x-p"/> One (of these pupils) then went to the field to gather vegetables (ארת, <hi type="italic">olera:</hi> for the different explanations of this word see Celsii <hi type="italic">Hierobot</hi>. i. 459ff., and Ges. <hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 56), and found שׂדה גּפן, i.e., not wild vines, but wild creepers (Luther), field-creepers resembling vines; and having gathered his lap full of wild cucumbers, took them home and cut them into the vegetable pot. because they did not know them. פּקּעת is rendered in the ancient versions <hi type="italic">colocynths</hi> (lxx πολυπὴ ἀγρία, i.e., according to Suid., <hi type="italic">Colocynthis</hi>), whereas Gesenius (<hi type="italic">Thes</hi>. p. 1122), Winer, and others, follow Celsius (<hi type="italic">l.c</hi>. i. 393ff.), have decided in favour of wild cucumbers, a fruit resembling an acorn, or, according to Oken, a green fleshy fruit of almost a finger’s length and an inch thick, which crack with a loud noise, when quite ripe, and very gentle pressure, spirting out both juice and seeds, and have a very bitter taste. The reason for this decision is, that the peculiarity mentioned answers to the etymon פּקע, to split, in Syr. and Chald. to crack. Nevertheless the rendering given by the old translators is apparently the more correct of the two; for the colocynths also belong to the genus of the cucumbers, creep upon the ground, and are a round yellow fruit of the size of a large orange, and moreover are extremely bitter, producing colic, and affecting the nerves. The form of this fruit is far more suitable for oval architectural ornaments (פּקעים,   1Ki 6:18; 1Ki 7:24) than that of the wild cucumber.
entries.0e2644ced02cbaa24747d4be7c70a8c575745c8a: 2Ki 4:40 <div eID="gen5181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5182" type="x-p"/> The extremely bitter flavour of the fruit so alarmed the pupils of the prophets when they began to eat of the dish, that they cried out, “Death in the pot,” and therefore thought the fruit was poison. If eaten in any large quantity, colocynths might really produce death: vid., Dioscorid. iv. 175 (178).
entries.fc13400cbc6922009c37bee2773769740ca23600: 2Ki 4:41 <div eID="gen5182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5183" type="x-p"/> Elisha then had some meal brought and poured it into the pot, after which the people were able to eat of the dish, and there was no longer anything injurious in the pot. וּקחוּ, then take, וּ denoting sequence in thought (vid., Ewald, §348, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.). The meal might somewhat modify the bitterness and injurious qualities of the vegetable, but could not take them entirely away; the author of the <hi type="italic">Exegetical Handbook</hi> therefore endeavours to get rid of the miracle, by observing that Elisha may have added something else. The meal, the most wholesome food of man, was only the earthly substratum for the working of the Spirit, which proceeded from Elisha, and made the noxious food perfectly wholesome.
entries.1e777308808670b73b38d3ea557022c2dc3d5b03: 2Ki 4:42-44 <div eID="gen5183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5184" type="x-p"/> Feeding of a Hundred Pupils of the Prophets with Twenty Barley Loaves. - A man of <hi type="italic">Baal-Shalisha</hi> (a place in the land of <hi type="italic">Shalisha</hi>, the country to the west of Gilgal, Jiljilia; see at <reference osisRef="1Sam.9.4">1Sa 9:4</reference>) brought the prophet as first-fruits twenty barley loaves and כּרמל = כּרמל גּרשׂ, i.e., roasted ears of corn (see the Comm. on <reference osisRef="Lev.2.14">Lev 2:14</reference>), in his sack (צקלון, ἁπ. λεγ., sack or pocket). Elisha ordered this present to be given to the people, i.e., to the pupils of the prophets who dwelt in one common home, for them to eat; and when his servant made this objection: “How shall I set this (this little) before a hundred men?” he repeated his command, “Give it to the people, that they may eat; for thus hath the Lord spoken: They will eat and leave” (והותר אכול, <hi type="italic">infin. absol</hi>.; see Ewald, §328, <hi type="italic">a</hi>.); which actually was the case. That twenty barley loaves and a portion of roasted grains of corn were not a sufficient quantity to satisfy a hundred men, is evident from the fact that one man was able to carry the whole of this gift in a sack, and still more so from the remark of the servant, which shows that there was no proportion between the whole of this quantity and the food required by a hundred persons. In this respect the food, which was so blessed by the word of the Lord that a hundred men were satisfied by so small a quantity and left some over, forms a type of the miraculous feeding of the people by Christ (Mat 14:16., 2Ki 15:36-37; Joh 6:11-12); though there was this distinction between them, that the prophet Elisha did not produce the miraculous increase of the food, but merely predicted it. The object, therefore, in communicating this account is not to relate another miracle of Elisha, but to show how the Lord cared for His servants, and assigned to them that which had been appropriated in the law to the Levitical priests, who were to receive, according to <reference osisRef="Deut.18.4-Deut.18.5">Deu 18:4-5</reference>, and Num 18:13, the first-fruits of corn, new wine, and oil. This account therefore furnishes fresh evidence that the godly men in Israel did not regard the worship introduced by Jeroboam (his state-church) as legitimate worship, but sought and found in the schools of the prophets a substitute for the lawful worship of God (vid., <hi type="italic">Hengstenberg</hi>, <hi type="italic">Beitrr</hi>. ii. S. 136f.).  <chapter eID="2Kgs.4"/> <div eID="gen5184" type="x-p"/>

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. IV.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p>NOw there cried a certain woman of the wives of the sons of the prophets <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Who, though they were wholly devoted to Sacred em<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ployment, were not excluded from Marriage, no more than the Priests and <ns0:hi>Levites.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note> unto El sha, saying, Thy servant my husband is dead, and thou knowest that thy servant did fear the LORD <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">His poverty therefore was not procured by his idleness, or prodigality, or rather, wicked<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness; but by his Piety, because he would not comply with the Kings way of worship, and therefore lost all worldly advantages.</ns0:note>: and the creditor is come to take unto him my two sons to be bond-men <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Either, to use them as his slaves, or to sell them to others, according to his Law.                   <ns0:p n="2">2 And Elisha said unto her, What shall I do for thee <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">How shall I relieve thee, who am my self poor?</ns0:note>? Tell me, what hast thou in the house <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Which may contribute to the Payment of thy Debts, or, at least, to the satisfaction of thy Creditors, who may per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chance deal favourably with thee through my persuasion.</ns0:note>? And she said, Thine hand-maid <ns0:hi>hath</ns0:hi> not any thing in the house, save a pot of oil <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Which was useful for divers things about the Service of God, and health, or delight, or ornament, and other uses of men. See <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 9. 9.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3 Then he said, Go, borrow thee vessels abroad of all thy neighbours, <ns0:hi>even</ns0:hi> empty vessels, <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> 
                        <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> not.</ns0:note> borrow not a few.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 And when thou art come in, thou shalt shut the door upon thee <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">Partly, that none may hinder thee from minding thy work of filling and removing the Vessels, which will require attention and diligence: partly, that thou alone maist enjoy the benefit of it: partly, lest any of thy Creditors should break in upon thee, and seize upon thy borrowed Vessels be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore they are filled: partly, that thy mind being freed from distraction, may be wholly employed in Prayer and Praising of God: and partly, that it may be manifest that this is the work of God alone.</ns0:note>, and upon thy sons, and shalt pour out <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Out of the Pot, in which God mul<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tiplied the Oil from time to time.</ns0:note> into all those vessels, and thou shalt set aside that which is full.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 So she went from him, and shut the door up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on her, and upon her sons: who brought <ns0:hi>the vessels</ns0:hi> to her, and she poured out.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 And it came to pass when the vessels were full,
<ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:303" />
that she said unto her son <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To one of them: for she had two, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 1.</ns0:note>, Bring me yet a vessel. And he said unto her, <ns0:hi>There is</ns0:hi> not a vessel more. And the oil stayed <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">To teach us, that we should not waste any of Gods Good Creatures; and that God would not work Miracles unnecessarily.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Then she came and told the man of God: and he said, Go, sell the oil, and pay thy <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> creditor.</ns0:note> debt, and live thou and thy children of the rest <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">First do Justice to others, and then take care of thy self and Children.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 ¶ And <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> there was a day.</ns0:note> it <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                        <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ell on a day, that Elisha passed to Shunem <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">A City in <ns0:hi>Issachar,</ns0:hi> near Mount <ns0:hi>Carmel, Ios.</ns0:hi> 19. 17, 18. whither the Prophet frequently went.</ns0:note>, where <ns0:hi>was</ns0:hi> a great woman <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">For Estate, or Birth and Quality. See <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 24. 35. 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 25. 2.</ns0:note>; and she <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> laid <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>old on him.</ns0:note> constrained him <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">By her importunate desire.</ns0:note> to eat bread <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">To take his repast there.</ns0:note>. And so it was, that as oft as he passed by, he turned in thi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther to eat bread.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 And she said unto her husband, Behold, now I perceive, that this <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> an holy man of God <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">A Prophet, as <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 13. 6. and that of eminent Holi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness: by our kindness to whom, we shall procure a blessing to our selves.</ns0:note>, which passeth by us continually.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10 Let us make a little chamber, I pray thee, on the wall <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">That he may be free from the noise of Family-business, and enjoy that privacy, which, I perceive, he desireth for his Prayers and Meditations.</ns0:note>, and let us set for him there a bed, and a table, and a stool, and a candlestick <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">He will not be troublesome or thargeable to us: he cares not for rich Furniture or costly Entertainment, and is content with bare necessaries.</ns0:note>: and it shall be when he cometh to us, that he shall turn in thither.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="11">11 And it fell on a day that he came thither, and he turned into the chamber, and lay there.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="12">12 And he said to Gehazi his servant, Call this Shunammite. And when he had called her, she stood before him <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Before the Prophet, <ns0:hi>in the door</ns0:hi> of his Chamber, as it is said, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 15. The relation seems to be a little perplexed, but may be thus conceived. It is in this Verse recorded in the general, That the Prophet sent <ns0:hi>Gehazi</ns0:hi> to call her, and that the came to him upon that call: then follows a parti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cular description of the whole business with all the circum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stances, first, of the message with which <ns0:hi>Gehazi</ns0:hi> was sent when he went to call her, and of her answer to that message, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 13. and of <ns0:hi>Gehazi's</ns0:hi> conjecture thereupon, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 14. and then of her coming to the Prophet at his call: which is there repeated to make way for the following passages.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="13">13 And he said <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> had said.</ns0:note> unto him, Say now unto her, Behold, thou hast been careful for us with all this care, What <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> to be done for thee <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Where with shall I recompence all thy care and kindness to me and my Servant?</ns0:note>? Wouldest thou be spoken for to the king, or to the captain of the host <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">With whom he justly had great power for his eminent service, <ns0:hi>chap.</ns0:hi> 3.</ns0:note>? And she answered, I dwell among mine own people <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">I live in Love and Peace among my Kindred and Friends; nor have I any cause to complain of them, or to seek relief from higher powers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="14">14 And he said, What then <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> to be done for her <ns0:note place="bottom">Hast thou observed any thing which she wants or de<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sires? For the Prophet kept himself much in his Chamber, whilst <ns0:hi>Gehazi</ns0:hi> went more freely about the House, as his oc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />casions led him.</ns0:note>? And Gehazi answered, Verily she hath no child, and her husband is old.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="15">15 And he said, Call her. And when he had cal<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />led her, she stood in the door <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Out of reverence, humility, and modesty, waiting till he came to her, or called her further in to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="16">16 And he said, About this <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> set time.</ns0:note> season, according to the time of life <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">Of which Phrase see on <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 18. 10.</ns0:note>, thou shalt imbrace a son. And she said, Nay, my lord, <ns0:hi>thou</ns0:hi> man of God, do not lye unto thine hand-maid <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Do not delude me with vain hopes. She could not believe it for joy, and supposed the Prophet might say thus either for her trial, or from his own private judgment and affection, and not by warrant from God.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="17">17 And the woman conceived and bare a son, at that season that Elisha had said unto her, accord<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing to the time of life.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="18">18 ¶ And when the child was grown, it fell on a day, that he went out to his father to the reap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ers.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="19">19 And he said to his father, My head, my head <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">His Head was grievously pained: which possibly came from the heat of the Harvest-season, to which he was ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed in the field.</ns0:note>: and he said to a lad, Carry him to his mother.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="20">20 And when he had taken him, and brought him to his mother, he sat on her knees till noon, and <ns0:hi>then</ns0:hi> died.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="21">21 And she went up, and laid him on the bed of the man of God, and shut <ns0:hi>the door</ns0:hi> upon him <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Partly, in hopes that this might contribute something to the Childs restitution to Life, she having in all probabili<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ty had an account of the like Miracle done by <ns0:hi>Elijah,</ns0:hi> 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 17. 21. and partly, that she might for the present conceal the death of the Child: which if it had been known, would have filled her Husband with grief, and hindred her journey, and opened the mouths of the enemies of God and his Prophets to blaspheme: whereas she had a confidence put into her by God, that the Prophet could and would re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />store her Son.</ns0:note>, and went out.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="22">22 And she called unto her husband, and said, Send me, I pray thee, one of the young men, and one of the asses, that I may run to the man of God, and come again.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="23">23 And he said, Wherefore wilt thou go to him to day? <ns0:hi>it is</ns0:hi> neither new moon nor sabbath <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Which were the chief and usual times in which they resorted to the Prophets for instruction, for which he sup<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posed she now went, not suspecting but that the Child was well by this time.</ns0:note>. And she said, <ns0:hi>It shall be</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> peace.</ns0:note> well <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">My going will not be troublesome to him, no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> prejudicial to thee or me. Heb. <ns0:hi>peace,</ns0:hi> i. e. peace be to thee, farewel, or be contented, let me go.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="24">24 Then she sadled an ass, and said to her ser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vant, Drive, and go forward: <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> restrain not for me to ride.</ns0:note> slack not <ns0:hi>thy</ns0:hi> riding for me, except I bid thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="25">25 So she went, and came unto the man of God to mount Carmel: and it came to pass when the man of God saw her asar off, that he said to Ge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hazi his servant, Behold, <ns0:hi>yonder is</ns0:hi> that Shunam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mite:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="26">26 Run now, I pray thee, to meet her, and say unto her, <ns0:hi>Is it</ns0:hi> well with thee? <ns0:hi>Is it</ns0:hi> well with thy husband? <ns0:hi>Is it</ns0:hi> well with the child? And she an<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />swered, <ns0:hi>It is</ns0:hi> well <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">So it was in some respects, because it was the Will of a Wise and Good God, and therefore best for her. Or, it shall be <ns0:hi>well:</ns0:hi> though the Child be dead, I doubt not by Gods blessing upon thy endeavours it shall live again and do well. But she answers ambiguously, and briefly too, that she might sooner come to the Prophet, and more fully open her mind to him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">27 And when she came to the man of God to the hill, she caught <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> by his feet.</ns0:note> him by the feet <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">She fell at his Feet and touched them, as a most hum<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ble and earnest suppliant. Compare 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 25. 24. <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 28. 9. Withal, she intimated, what she durst <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>ot presume to express in words, that she desired him to go along with her.</ns0:note>: but Geha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />zi came near to thrust her away <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Judging this posture indecent for her, and offensive to her Master.</ns0:note>. And the man of God said, Let her alone, for her soul <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> bitter.</ns0:note> vexed within her <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Disturb her not, for this uncouth gesture is a sign of some extraordinary grief.</ns0:note>: and the LORD hath hid <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> from me, and hath not told me <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">Whereby he signifies, that what he knew or did, was not by any vertue inherent and abiding in himself, but onely from God, who revealed to him onely what and when he pleased. Compare 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 7. 3.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:304" />28 Then she said, Did I desire a son of my lord <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">This Child was not given to me upon my immoderate desire, for which I might have justly been thus chastised, as <ns0:hi>Rachel</ns0:hi> was, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 30. 1. compare with 35. 18. but was free<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly promised to me by thee in Gods Name, and from his spe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cial Grace and Favour: and therefore I trust both thou didst pray for it, and God design it as a blessing, and not as an affli<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ction, as now it proves, unless thou dost obtain the Child for me a second time, which I know thou canst do, and I humbly beg thee to do.</ns0:note>? Did not I say, Do not deceive me <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">With vain hopes of a comfort that I should never have. And I had been much happier if I had never had it, than to lose it so quickly. Therefore thou art in some measure concerned to revive my dead hopes, and to continue to me the great blessing which thou hast procured.</ns0:note>?</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="29">29 Then he said to Gehazi, Gird up thy loins <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Tie up thy long Garments about thy Loins for ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pedition. See 1 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 18. 46.</ns0:note>, and take my staff in thy hand, and go thy way: if thou meet any man, salute him not: and if any salute thee, answer him not again <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">An Hyperbolical ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression: Make no delays nor stops by the way, neither by words nor actions, but go with all possible speed. Compare <ns0:hi>Luk.</ns0:hi> 10. 4. He requires this haste, that the Miracle might be done secretly and speedily before the Childs death was di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vulged, which might cause many inconveniences. See on <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 21.</ns0:note>: and lay my staff upon the face of the child <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">For God can work a Miracle by the most unlikely and contemptible means, as he did by a Rod, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 14. 16. and a Mantle, 2 <ns0:hi>King.</ns0:hi> 2. 8.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="30">30 And the mother of the child said, <ns0:hi>As</ns0:hi> the LORD liveth, and <ns0:hi>as</ns0:hi> thy soul liveth, I will not leave thee <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Until thou goest home with me. For she had no great confidence in <ns0:hi>Gehazi,</ns0:hi> nor was her Faith so strong as to think that the Prophet could work so great a Miracle at this distance, and by his Staff: which possibly was one rea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />son why this did no good. Compare <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 9. 18. and 13. 58. and 17. 20.</ns0:note>. And he arose and followed her.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="31">31 And Gehazi passed on before them, and laid the staff upon the face of the child, but <ns0:hi>there was</ns0:hi> neither voice, nor <ns0:note n="‡" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> atten<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion.</ns0:note> hearing <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Neither speech, nor sense, nor any sign of life, to wit, in the Child. Which disappointment might proceed from hence, that <ns0:hi>Elisha</ns0:hi> having changed his mind, and yield<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to her importunity to go with her, did alter his course, and not joyn his fervent prayers with <ns0:hi>Gehazi</ns0:hi>'s action, but re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served them till he came thither.</ns0:note>: wherefore he went again to meet him, and told him, saying, The child <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> not awaked <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Not revived: death being oft and fitly compared to a sleep, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 76. 5. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 12. 2. because of the Resurrection which will in due time follow it, and here followed speedily, which makes the expression most proper in this place.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="32">32 And when Elisha was come into the house, behold, the child was dead, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> laid upon his bed.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="33">33 He went in therefore, and shut the door up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on them twain <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Upon himself and the dead Child, that he might pray to God without distraction, and might more freely use all those gestures and means which he thought fit.</ns0:note>, and prayed unto the LORD.</ns0:p>
